title: Psalm 27 in Elul
hook: said through the month before the High Holy Days: wait for the Lord, be strong

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm one twenty-one and the keeper on the night shift. Your line was he doesn't sleep. Did you let someone else hold the night? Day three hundred twenty-six.

Athletes have a preseason. Actors have rehearsals. Before a wedding there are weeks of fittings and planning and nerves. Nobody walks into the big day cold. The Jewish year works the same way. Before the High Holy Days, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, there's a whole month of warming up. It has its own sounds: the shofar blown in the morning. And its own psalm, said every day, twice a day in many communities. Today's word is the name of that month: Elul.
screen: `A PRESEASON, A REHEARSAL.` → `NOBODY WALKS IN COLD.` → `A MONTH TO WARM UP.`

segments.voice: Elul is the last month of the Jewish year, the month right before Rosh Hashanah. It's a month for turning around, teshuvah, getting ready to stand before God. Tradition hears a hint in its four letters: aleph, lamed, vav, lamed. They're the first letters of a line from the Song of Songs: ani le-dodi ve-dodi li, I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine. So Elul isn't only a time of fear. It's a time of closeness. And every day of Elul, many communities add Psalm twenty-seven. It opens with courage: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?" An old midrash reads the psalm as a map of the season ahead. My light: that's Rosh Hashanah. My salvation: that's Yom Kippur. And later, when the psalm says God will hide me in His shelter, the Hebrew word is sukkah: the festival of Sukkot that comes after. The psalm goes through the whole holiday season. But it's honest, too. The middle of the psalm gets shaky. Hide not Your face from me. Even if my father and mother leave me. It isn't the voice of someone who has it all together. And then the last line, the one Elul hangs on: "Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let thy heart take courage; yea, wait thou for the LORD." Wait, then be strong, then wait again. Getting ready isn't about having answers. It's about staying, with courage, until the day comes.
screen: `ELUL: THE MONTH BEFORE.` · `I AM MY BELOVED'S.` · `LIGHT, SALVATION, SHELTER.` · `WAIT, BE STRONG, WAIT.` · then, large: `WAIT, AND BE STRONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Psalm twenty-seven once. If you can, find it, and read it slowly, all fourteen verses. Notice where it's brave and where it trembles. If you can't, sit with its first and last lines. Settle, and breathe. The Lord is my light; whom shall I fear? Let one fear come up. Then the last line: wait, and be strong. You don't have to solve the fear today. Just wait beside it, with a little courage. If you pray, you can say the psalm as your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Elul. The month before the High Holy Days: I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine. Its psalm ends: wait for the Lord, be strong.
Your line: wait, and be strong. Today, when something big is coming and you feel unready, take one small step to prepare, and let your heart take courage. Day three hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: From the start of Elul through the High Holy Day season, many communities add Psalm 27 to morning and afternoon or evening prayers, and Ashkenazi communities blow the shofar each weekday morning of Elul.

original.note: Hebrew: the sixth month, counting from Nisan, and the last before Rosh Hashanah.

trapdoor: what you thought: a month on the Jewish calendar.
what it means: a month of turning and closeness before the High Holy Days, carried by Psalm 27.
what a scholar hears: the acronym from Song of Songs 6:3 is a later homiletic reading, and Vayikra Rabbah 21:4 maps Psalm 27 onto Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.

notes: Psalm 27:1 and 27:14 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm wording.
Vayikra Rabbah 21:4 (light = Rosh Hashanah, salvation = Yom Kippur); the Sukkot link from 'sukkah' in 27:5 is a later addition (e.g., in the Mateh Ephraim / common teaching). Confirm.
Custom: Psalm 27 from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Hoshana Rabbah or Shemini Atzeret, twice daily in many Ashkenazi communities; Sephardi practice varies. Confirm.
The Elul acronym from Song of Songs 6:3 is a later homiletic reading.
